# LLM Optimization: How to Maximize LLM Performance

![Brain John Aboze](/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/avatar-96x96.png) Brain John Aboze

| March 02, 2026 |   13 mins

Subscribe to the newsletter

This blog post was written by Brain John Aboze as part of the Deepchecks Community Blog. If you would like to contribute your own blog post, feel free to reach out to us via [blog@deepchecks.com](mail:blog@deepchecks.com). We typically pay a symbolic fee for content that's accepted by our reviewers.

## LLM Optimization: How to Maximize LLM Performance

Building a prototype for a Large Language Model (LLM) application can be exciting and facile. Getting it ready for production settings, however, can be fraught with challenges. Foundation models are often built for general use but often need optimization or improvements when confronted with required customization for domain-specific requirements, knowledge, systems integration, or processes. It is crucial to note that optimizing [LLMs](/glossary/llm-parameters/) is a complex iterative process with elements that require an approach fitted to the intended model functions and operating context. To bridge these gaps, core optimization strategies to maximize [LLM performance](/llm-evaluation-metrics/) in diverse use cases will be covered in this article.

![How to Maximize LLM Performance ](/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/img-how-to-maximize-llm-performance.jpg)

Photo by [Ivan Samkov](https://www.pexels.com/photo/man-using-a-laptop-at-a-wood-workshop-4491881/)

For optimization to be possible, evaluation must be put in place to guide efforts and assess impact. As Peter F. Drucker said, “You can’t manage what you don’t measure.”  A robust evaluation framework is crucial for guiding LLM optimization efforts, as it helps identify the model’s shortcomings and uncover insights to guide the optimization strategy.

You can read more about LLM-based application evaluation [[LLM-based Application Evaluation](/llm-based-application-evaluation/)].

## Types of LLM Optimization

When people say “LLM optimization,” they often mean very different things. In practice, it helps to group techniques by the part of the system they modify: the prompt, the retrieved data, the model weights, or the inference and serving stack. Thinking in these buckets keeps you from “optimizing” in circles and pushes you toward changes that actually move your metrics.

![Types of LLM Optimization](/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/img-types-llm-optimization.jpg)

Source: By Author

### 1. Behavior-level optimization (prompt and policy)

This bucket focuses on shaping model behavior without modifying the underlying weights. It’s usually the fastest path to improved performance because you’re adjusting how the system asks questions and how it accepts answers, rather than retraining anything.

In practice, teams tighten prompt templates (system/developer/user structure), enforce output schemas (e.g., strict JSON or function-call style), and add guardrails that constrain refusal behavior, safety boundaries, or tool-use rules. The difference-maker is measurement: prompt versioning and [A/B testing](/llm-evaluation/) turn “prompt tweaking” into actual optimization, by letting you verify improvements rather than guess. Early on, this is often the cheapest and most reliable lever you have.

### 2. Knowledge grounding optimization (RAG)

If the model is “smart but forgetful,” the bottleneck may be what it can look up rather than what it can reason about. [Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)](/retrieval-augmented-generation-best-practices-and-use-cases/) improves accuracy and freshness by providing the model with stronger, cleaner context at the time of response.

![Knowledge grounding optimization (RAG)](/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/img-knowledge-grounding-optimization.jpg)

Source: [System-level RAG Pipeline](https://dextralabs.com/blog/rag-pipeline-explained-diagram-implementation/)

Most RAG improvements come down to reducing noise and increasing signal. That might mean better chunking and metadata to ensure retrieval pulls the right passages, query rewriting or expansion to align with the knowledge base’s language, and reranking or filtering to ensure only the highest-value context reaches the model. Once retrieval is working well, context compression (summaries or extracted snippets) can reduce token costs while preserving the important evidence. The trade-off is that RAG can introduce latency and operational complexity, so many production systems pair it with caching and routing to keep response times stable.

### 3. Model adaptation optimization (fine-tuning and PEFT)

When your task has stable patterns, and you have a solid dataset, it can be more effective to adapt the model than to keep stacking prompt instructions. Fine-tuning often turns a “clever demo” into consistent, repeatable outputs, especially for domain-specific language, tone, and formatting.

Instruction tuning helps the model reliably follow your domain-specific behaviors. [PEFT approaches (adapter-based methods)](/glossary/parameter-efficient-fine-tuning/) reduce training and storage costs, making adaptation more practical. And when cost or latency dominates, distillation can be a strong strategy: you train a smaller model to imitate a larger one, preserving much of the behavior while reducing serving costs.

A good signal that tuning is worth it is when prompts keep getting longer to “force” a consistent format, yet the output still drifts under real user variability.

### 4. Runtime optimization (LLM inference)

This is LLM inference optimization: improving generation speed and reducing memory usage during serving. It’s often the difference between something that works in a demo and something that can handle real traffic without blowing up your latency budget.

If you self-host, common approaches include [quantization](/glossary/llm-quantization/) (e.g., 8-bit or 4-bit) to reduce memory footprint and accelerate compute in many setups, attention optimizations such as [Flash Attention](https://flashattn.dev/blog/flash-attention-complete-guide) for long contexts, and serving-phase tuning based on how generation behaves across prefill vs. decode. [Batching strategies and KV-cache](/question/how-does-llm-inference-work/) management are also key because they keep GPUs busy and reduce per-token cost.

![Runtime optimization (LLM inference)](/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/img-runtime-optimization.jpg)

Source: [An illustration of the key-value caching mechanism](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/)

Even if you’re using an API model and can’t change kernels, the same “runtime thinking” applies. You can limit token budgets, reduce the size of retrieved payloads, cache repeated answers, and route easier requests to smaller models. These are all runtime optimizations in practice because they directly reduce the amount of work per request.

### 5. System-level optimization (architecture and ops)

This is where teams quietly win. Many real-world improvements come from system design rather than model changes, especially once you’re past early prototyping.

Response caching (exact-match and semantic caching for near-duplicates) can eliminate entire model calls for repeated questions. Request routing can push simpler queries to cheaper models while reserving expensive calls for the cases that truly need them. Tool-call optimization matters too: reduce unnecessary calls, parallelize safe tool calls, and track tool latency separately from generation latency. Observability ties it all together by giving you a breakdown of where time is spent across retrieval, generation, and tools, so you’re not “optimizing” the wrong piece. Finally, guarded fallbacks prevent brittle systems: if retrieval fails, return a safe partial answer rather than a confident hallucination.

## Core Optimization Strategies

## Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering is designing inputs that guide
